pron_note: Short "a" as in cat — not im-PLAY-kuh-buhl, a common slip.
means:
Impossible to appease, soften, or talk round — hostility or opposition that no apology, concession, or plea will touch.

The force of the word is in what *doesn't* work on it. An angry person can be calmed; an implacable one cannot, and that's the point — it describes a permanent setting, not a mood. So it carries weight rather than pettiness: implacable enemies, implacable hatred, implacable opposition. It stretches easily to impersonal things that simply keep coming — the implacable advance of the tide, of age, of the deadline — and when applied to a person's *resolve* rather than their malice, it can even read as admiring.
trap: ⚠️ **implacable ≠ impeccable.** Near-identical on the page and in the ear, opposite in feel: **implacable** = cannot be appeased; **impeccable** = flawless (Latin *peccare*, "to sin" — literally *sinless*).
trick_unpack: The word wears its own test: *placate* means to soothe with concessions, and this is the person on whom concessions are wasted.
sentences: Two apologies and a resignation did nothing; the committee remained **implacable**.
She's been **implacable** about that parking space since 2019 — don't even try.
in_the_wild: Kyle Reese's warning in **The Terminator** is the finest definition of *implacable* ever filmed: *"It can't be bargained with. It can't be reasoned with. It doesn't feel pity, or remorse, or fear. And it absolutely will not stop, ever, until you are dead."*
etymology:
Latin **placāre** = *"to soothe, calm down"* + **in-** (*not*). Literally: **un-soothe-able.**

Same root pays out across the exam: **placate** (soothe), **placid** (soothed, calm), **complacent** (smugly pleased and therefore idle), **placebo** (*"I shall please"*).
one_line: Impossible to appease; relentlessly hostile or unstoppable.
